founded.what: The year an alderman of Aÿ of the Gosset family set up a wine business there, making still wines, most of them red, by the house.

place: Aÿ, then Épernay from 2009, Vallée de la Marne, Champagne

kind.means: A négociant manipulant, a house in the trade's own word: it buys grapes from growers beyond any vines of its own and makes the wine itself, and the Union des Maisons de Champagne lists it among the houses.

story: Gosset dates itself from 1584, when an alderman of Aÿ of the Gosset family set up a wine business there. By the house's account he made still wines, most of them red, from his own vines: Champagne was not yet sparkling, so Gosset calls itself the oldest wine house of Champagne, not the oldest house of sparkling Champagne. The family ran it at Aÿ for generations; by its own account a woman of the family who led the house from 1955 to 1965 was the first to present a rosé Champagne in a clear bottle. At the end of 1993 the house joined the group of the Renaud-Cointreau family, by its own pages and the Union des Maisons de Champagne. The 1988 vintage gave the first Celebris, sold from 1995: the house later counted the 2012 as only the ninth Celebris in thirty five years. In 2009 the house moved to Épernay, to an estate with listed parkland and cellars of the nineteenth century, while keeping its name of Aÿ. Its mark is the avoided malolactic conversion, which keeps the wines' natural acidity and their fruit, and long ageing on the lees, four years on average by its own charter.

style.line: Fresh, taut and vinous: the house avoids the malolactic conversion to keep the wine's natural acidity and fruit, and ages it long on its lees, giving lemon peel, quince and a firm, long finish.
style.grapes: Pinot Noir and Chardonnay lead, bought from growers across the Grand and Premier Cru villages; Grande Réserve adds Meunier, at about a fifth, by the house.
style.malolactic: Avoided, by the house's page for Grande Réserve, to keep the fruit; the importer says the same of Celebris, made without barrels or malolactic.
style.lees: Four years on average across the range, by the house's charter; Grande Réserve at least four years, Celebris twelve for the 2008.
style.dosage: Grande Réserve 6 grams a litre by the house's technical sheet, adjusted with care, and the bottles rest at least six months after disgorging.

nv.name: Grande Réserve
nv.note: The non vintage Brut: Pinot Noir, Chardonnay and Meunier, at least four years on its lees, made without the malolactic conversion.

cuvee.name: Celebris

first.what: The first vintage, sold from 1995, by a tasting report and the house's own count of its vintages.

cuvee.rhythm: Made only in chosen years: the house called the 2008 the eighth Celebris and the 2012 the ninth in thirty five years. Other vintages read are the 1990, 1995, 2002, 2004 and 2007.
cuvee.blend: Chardonnay and Pinot Noir, Chardonnay leading, from a little over half to about seven tenths by the vintage; no Meunier.
cuvee.sites: Grand and Premier Cru villages of the Côte des Blancs, the Montagne de Reims and the Vallée de la Marne: for the 2008, Ambonnay, Avenay, Avize, Aÿ, Bouzy, Cramant, Cuis, Cumières, Trépail, Vertus and Le Mesnil-sur-Oger.
cuvee.making: Made without barrels and without the malolactic conversion, by the house's importer, so the natural acidity stays whole. It ages for over a decade on its lees and rests after disgorging. The dosage has moved: 4.8 grams a litre for the 2008, an Extra Brut, while the 2012 is labelled Brut.
cuvee.lees: Twelve years for the 2008, by the house's importer; the house speaks of a prolonged maturing on the lees.
cuvee.young: Pear cake, vanilla madeleine and sabayon by the house's own note, with orange oil, almond pastry and peach by a critic, over a long, salty finish.
cuvee.aged: It is released already mature after more than a decade in the cellar; no note read follows a bottle long after release, so none is told here.

forms.name: Celebris Rosé
forms.note: A vintage rosé of the same name, the 2008 an Extra Brut, by the house's importer.

forms.name: Celebris Blanc de Blancs
forms.note: A vintage of Chardonnay alone under the same name, made in the 2012.

cuvee.serve: 9 to 11 degrees Celsius, never ice cold; no need to decant; a white wine glass, so the long aged wine can open.

table.house45: Gosset is the oldest wine house in Champagne, dating itself from 1584 at Aÿ. Back then it made still wines, mostly red, long before Champagne sparkled. The house has one clear signature: it keeps its wines from softening their sharp natural acid, so they stay fresh, taut and full of fruit. It also ages them long, four years on average across the range, which rounds them out. In 2009 it moved to an estate in Épernay with cellars of the nineteenth century. Most guests know Grande Réserve, and the prestige cuvée is Celebris.
table.house10: Gosset is the oldest wine house in Champagne, from 1584 at Aÿ, known for wines kept fresh and taut by their natural acid.
table.cuvee45: Celebris is the vintage prestige cuvée of Gosset, first made in 1988. It is Chardonnay and Pinot Noir from Grand and Premier Cru villages, with Chardonnay leading. What sets it apart is freshness: the wine keeps all its sharp natural acid, never softened and never put in barrels, and then it ages more than a decade before release. The 2012 was only the ninth vintage in thirty five years. Expect pear cake, vanilla and almond pastry over a long, salty finish. I serve it at about ten degrees in a white wine glass.
table.sale: For a guest who likes Champagne with real freshness and age, Celebris is Gosset's vintage wine, kept taut by its own acidity and aged over a decade. May I bring a bottle for the table?
table.cuvee10: Celebris is Gosset's vintage prestige cuvée, Chardonnay led, kept fresh by its natural acid and aged more than a decade.
table.cuvee20: Celebris is the vintage prestige cuvée of Gosset, Chardonnay and Pinot Noir from Grand and Premier Cru villages. It keeps its natural acidity and ages more than a decade, which gives pear cake and almond pastry with a salty finish.

guests.q: Is Gosset the oldest Champagne house?
guests.a: It is the oldest wine house, from 1584, but it began with still wines. Ruinart, founded in 1729, is the oldest house of sparkling Champagne.

guests.q: What does no malolactic mean in the glass?
guests.a: The wine keeps its sharper natural acid instead of softening it, so it tastes fresher and tauter and keeps its fruit, and it needs long ageing to round out.
Some vintages are Extra Brut, the 2008 at under five grams of sugar a litre, while the 2012 is labelled Brut. Either way it tastes dry and fresh.

traps: Ruinart is the oldest Champagne house; Gosset is the oldest wine house but began with still wine.
Gosset is not Gosset-Brabant, a separate grower at Aÿ.
Gosset is dated to Aÿ in 1584 but moved to an estate at Épernay in 2009: both places are right, for different years.
Celebris is a vintage wine of Chardonnay and Pinot Noir; Grande Réserve, the non vintage Brut, is the one with Meunier.

sheet.label: Celebris
sheet.note: The sheet and the label agree. The label may add Extra Brut or Brut and the vintage, and a rosé and a Blanc de Blancs carry the same name.

questions.q: Which prestige cuvée on the class sheet is made by the house that dates itself from 1584?
questions.exp: Celebris is Gosset's, the oldest wine house of Champagne. Dom Ruinart is the prestige cuvée of Ruinart, of 1729, the oldest house of sparkling Champagne; Amour de Deutz is Deutz's and Grande Sendrée is Drappier's.

questions.q: What sets the Gosset house style apart in the cellar, by its own account?
opts: It ferments every wine in new oak
It adds no reserve wine to any blend
questions.exp: Gosset avoids the malolactic conversion to keep natural acidity and fruit. Old oak barrels are the mark of Bollinger, its old neighbour in Aÿ, and Gosset's own Grande Réserve blends Pinot Noir and Chardonnay with Meunier.

questions.q: Which grapes make Celebris, Gosset's vintage prestige cuvée?
opts: All seven grapes of the appellation
questions.exp: Celebris is Chardonnay led with Pinot Noir for the rest, from Grand and Premier Cru villages. Meunier goes into Grande Réserve, the non vintage Brut, and not into Celebris.

report: Built on the library's p-gosset and contradicting none of it: founded 1584, Aÿ then Épernay, malolactic blocked, Celebris the vintage prestige cuvée of Chardonnay and Pinot Noir, Grande Réserve the non vintage.
The library calls Celebris an Extra Brut at very low dosage: true of the 2008, but the importer labels the 2012 Brut, so the record says the dosage has moved.

The first vintage, 1988 sold from 1995, rests on one tasting report and on the house's own counts (the eighth in 34 years, the ninth in 35); the report's 1988 blend figures do not add up and are left out.
The founder and the woman who led the house from 1955 to 1965 are described and not named: their dates were not found in two sources.
The 1993 change of hands is dated to the end of 1993 by the house's own pages, beside the Union des Maisons de Champagne's listing of the group.
Gosset calls itself family owned and independent; the record tells only the dated history and leaves that present claim out.
style.reserve and style.vessels are empty: no house page read states them; the importer's no barrels is told for Celebris alone.
Celebris's malolactic and its twelve years on the lees rest on the importer's pages for the 2008, beside the house's own avoided malolactic for Grande Réserve.
The listed vintages 1990, 1995, 2002, 2004 and 2007 rest on critics' and merchants' listings; the full list of nine was not found, so none is counted beyond the house's own count.
cuvee.bottle is empty: no story of the bottle was sourced; the clear bottle of the rosé is told as the house's claim in the story.
kind.code: the letters NM were not read on a label; the union lists the house among its houses. A refuter should read a label.
Refuter: the 1993 change of hands is 1994 in a guide and a trade paper; the house and its importer say the end of 1993, which stands.

changed: cuvee.making: the 9 grams a litre for the 1988 rested on one report and is cut; 4.8 for the 2008 stands on the importer and Falstaff.
table.cuvee45: the house counts only nine vintages, true only until the next release, now reads the 2012 was only the ninth vintage in thirty five years (the Drinks Business, World of Fine Wine).

open: The founder is Pierre Gosset in the house's and the importer's accounts and Jean Gosset in one merchant's, which is why he stays described, not named.
The clear rosé bottle is dated 1947 by two trade accounts, before the woman's presidency of 1955 to 1965; the record keeps it undated as the house's claim.
Whether the 2012 label reads Brut or Extra Brut: the importer and one critic say Brut, a merchant Extra Brut.
NM was not read on a label.
